The must-sees

  • Barrio Santa Cruz

    Neighbourhood

    This was the city’s Jewish quarter until the violence of 1391 and the expulsion of 1492. Its lanes were tidied and romanticised in the early 20th century.

    Look for: The Callejón del Agua runs along the Alcázar’s garden wall, which once carried water pipes for the palace.

  • Giralda

    Landmark · 1198

    It was finished in 1198 as the minaret of the mosque, and ramps instead of stairs lead to the top. In the 16th century Hernán Ruiz added the belfry and the bronze weathervane, the Giraldillo.

    Look for: On each face of the Almohad shaft, find the sebka: a lattice of diamond-shaped brick panels.

  • María Luisa Park

    Park

    The Infanta María Luisa gave most of her palace gardens to the city in 1893. Jean-Claude Forestier redesigned them for the 1929 Exposition.

    Look for: Find the monument to the poet Bécquer: his bust above three marble women round a tree, showing the stages of love.

  • Metropol Parasol

    Building · 2011

    Locals call it Las Setas, the mushrooms, and it was designed by Jürgen Mayer. Roman remains found during construction are shown in a museum underneath.

    Look for: Under the canopy, at street level, the Encarnación market still sells fish, meat and vegetables.

  • Plaza de España

    Square · 1929

    Aníbal González designed it for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition. Tiled alcoves along the wall represent the provinces of Spain.

    Look for: The four bridges over the canal stand for the old kingdoms of Spain, with blue and white ceramic balustrades.

  • Real Maestranza Bullring

    Venue

    Construction began in 1749 and took more than a century to complete. It belongs to an old noble riding brotherhood and includes a museum.

    Look for: The Puerta del Príncipe is the gate through which a matador is carried shoulder-high after a great afternoon.

  • Royal Alcázar

    Palace

    Its core is the Mudéjar palace Pedro I had built in the 1360s by craftsmen from Granada and Toledo. The upper floors are still used by the Spanish royal family when in Seville.

    Look for: Over the Lion Gate, the entrance, a tiled heraldic lion holds a cross in its paw.

  • Seville Cathedral

    Church · 1506

    It was built from 1434 on the site of the city’s great mosque, keeping the minaret and the orange-tree courtyard. A monumental tomb inside holds remains attributed to Christopher Columbus.

    Look for: At Columbus’s tomb the coffin rides on the shoulders of four heralds, for the kingdoms of Castile, León, Aragon and Navarre.

  • Torre del Oro

    Fortress

    It was built in the early 13th century to guard the river, and a chain could be stretched from it to the far bank. Today it holds a small naval museum.

    Look for: Notice the three tiers: the twelve-sided base is Almohad, while the small round top was added in 1760.

  • Triana

    Neighbourhood

    For centuries Triana supplied the tiles that decorate Seville. Many of the sailors on the voyages to the Americas came from these streets.

    Look for: At the Triana end of the bridge, the small tiled Capillita del Carmen is nicknamed the lighter for its shape.

How it works

  1. Open Wizzy in Seville and tap Start walk, or pick a ready-made walk.
  2. Put your phone in your pocket. Wizzy runs in the background, even with the screen locked.
  3. When you pass a place, you get a ping. Open it for the story, or keep walking.

Every place you see gets stamped in your Seville passport. Your location stays on your phone. No ads, no tracking.
